title: Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Dunder Methods
description: Building class hierarchies, method overriding, polymorphism, properties, and Python's special (dunder) methods.
objectives: Use inheritance and super() to build class hierarchies
Use properties for controlled attribute access
Implement common dunder methods for operator overloading

content.heading: Inheritance and Polymorphism
content.body:
class Dog(Animal): makes Dog a subclass of Animal, inheriting its attributes and methods. A subclass can override a method by redefining it with the same name; super().method(...) calls the parent class's version, commonly used inside an overridden __init__ to run the parent's initialization logic before adding the subclass's own. Python also supports multiple inheritance (class C(A, B):) — when the same method name exists in multiple parent classes, Python resolves which one to use via the Method Resolution Order (MRO), a deterministic linearization of the class hierarchy (viewable with ClassName.__mro__).

Polymorphism means code can work with objects of different classes through a shared interface, calling the same method name and getting each object's own behavior — for example, iterating over a list of different Shape subclasses and calling .area() on each, without needing to know which concrete subclass each one is. Abstraction is often expressed with the abc module: an abstract base class can declare @abstractmethod methods that subclasses are required to implement, preventing the abstract class itself from being instantiated.

content.heading: Properties and Dunder (Magic) Methods
content.body:
The @property decorator lets a method be accessed like a plain attribute (obj.value instead of obj.value()), enabling computed attributes or validation logic on read, with an optional matching @value.setter for controlled writes — this gives Python-style 'getters and setters' without needing to expose separate get_x()/set_x() methods everywhere.

Dunder ('double underscore') methods let a class customize how its instances behave with built-in syntax and functions. __str__ controls what str(obj) and print(obj) show (a readable, user-facing representation); __repr__ controls the more precise, developer-facing representation shown in a REPL or inside a container. __len__ backs len(obj); __getitem__ and __iter__/__next__ let a custom object support indexing and iteration. Operator overloading is implemented the same way: __add__ defines what + does for your class's instances, __eq__ defines ==, and so on.

content.explanation: Calling .speak() on each object in the list demonstrates polymorphism — the same method call dispatches to each class's own implementation. __add__ makes the + operator work naturally between two Vector instances.

keyPoints: class Sub(Base): inherits from Base; super() calls the parent's version of an overridden method
Polymorphism lets different classes respond to the same method call, each in its own way
@property/@x.setter give controlled, attribute-like access to computed or validated values
Dunder methods (__str__, __eq__, __add__, __len__, __iter__, ...) let custom classes work with built-in syntax
commonMistakes: Overriding __init__ in a subclass without calling super().__init__(), leaving inherited attributes unset
Defining __eq__ without __hash__ and being surprised the object can no longer be used in a set or as a dict key
